What this guide pulls from Dr. Kemp Built from Dr. Walter Kemp's two-part Pathogenesis of Glomerular Clinicopathologic Syndromes (slides + narration; reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed.). I kept what he points at on the histology, IF and EM and the pathology rules he repeats (his "if you know the terminology, you know the name" approach). Practice questions sit at the end of each section; the summary table is last. beyond source = standard teaching points I added; corrected = source slip fixed.

2. Basic Responses to Injury

Proliferation

Cellular proliferation (top left), mesangial (top right), cellular crescents (bottom). Arrows are Kemp's.
TypeWhat it isKemp's examples / what you see
MesangialIncrease in mesangial matrix and/or cells (mesangium = the connective tissue between the twists and turns of the capillary loops)IgA nephropathy; diabetes
Cellular (intracapillary)More cells within the glomerulus; gives the tuft an overall lobular shapeMembranoproliferative GN (more cells = "proliferative")
CrescentsProliferation of epithelial cells in Bowman's space (between tuft and capsule); compresses the tuftYellow arrow in the figure. Normally the tuft fills Bowman's space

Membrane thickening

Top left: what the membrane should look like. The rest show varying thickening (arrows).
  • Thickening can be subtle on slides; H&E is usually not that useful for the basement membrane. Silver or PAS is used.
  • Especially known in membranous nephropathy: capillary loops in cross section look like thick-walled pipes ("wire loops").

Sclerosis

  • Sclerosis = scarring. Examples he gives: focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS); diabetic scarring of the mesangium (nodular).
NoteKemp calls these "responses to injury" that are nonspecific on their own. Specific diagnosis comes from combining them with IF and EM (Section 4).

3. Terminology: Diffuse, Focal, Segmental, Global

Diffuse (>50% of glomeruli): 3 of 3 involved, and the lower-right low-power view. Focal (<50%): one involved. Segmental: part of one glomerulus.
TermCounts...Meaning
Diffuseglomeruli (the sample)>50% of glomeruli involved (most or all)
Focalglomeruli<50% of glomeruli involved (some or few)
Globalwithin one glomerulusAll of that glomerulus involved
Segmentalwithin one glomerulusPart of that glomerulus involved
Read a name like a sentenceFocal segmental glomerulosclerosis = scarring (sclerosis) of some glomeruli (focal), and in each only part (segmental).

Glomerulonephritis vs glomerulonephropathy vs nephropathy

  • Glomerulonephritis: glomerular process with inflammation (-itis).
  • Glomerulonephropathy: glomerular process without inflammation.
  • Nephropathy: pathology of the kidney in general.
  • Usage isn't consistent: "membranous nephropathy" is the standard name even though it is a glomerular disease. Understand the meaning rather than the label.

Point to ponder

Can a pathologist call focal segmental sclerosis if only ONE glomerulus is on the biopsy?No. "Focal" vs "diffuse" needs several glomeruli to know what fraction is involved. With one glomerulus you can still say global (all of it) or segmental (part of it). A single fully scarred glomerulus = globally sclerotic.

4. Evaluating Glomerular Disease: Stains, IF and EM

Light microscopy and special stains

Same region by H&E, PAS, trichrome and silver stain.
StainHighlightsUse it for
H&EGeneral structureProliferation, crescents; not very useful for basement membrane
PAS (periodic acid-Schiff)Basement membrane (pinker)Membrane thickening
SilverBasement membrane (black)Thickening; spikes in membranous nephropathy
TrichromeFibrosis (blue)Scarring, e.g. nodular glomerulosclerosis in diabetes

Immunofluorescence (IF)

Granular capillary loop (top left), granular mesangial (top right), linear capillary loop (bottom left), crescent staining (bottom right).
  • Pattern: granular (little intermittent nodules = immune complexes) vs linear (a continuous band).
  • Distribution: mesangial vs capillary loop (it can also stain crescents).
  • Linear staining is seen only in anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome), which also involves the lungs. Everything else is granular.
  • IgA nephropathy: granular, mesangial. Post-infectious GN: usually capillary loops. Patterns can overlap and involve more than one compartment.

Electron microscopy (EM): where is the deposit?

Top left: subepithelial deposit (yellow; black arrows = podocyte foot processes). Top right: subendothelial deposits (white arrows; blue = basement membrane). Bottom left: mesangial deposit (yellow). Bottom right: dense deposit disease.
Kemp's drawing. Foot processes (blue columns) sit on the epithelial side.
  • Anchor on the podocyte foot processes (little columns coming down toward the basement membrane): deposits on that side are subepithelial; on the other side they are subendothelial. He considers this the most reliable thing to identify on EM.
  • Immune complexes are dark, round deposits.
  • Mesangial deposits sit in the central area where loops come together/overlap.
  • Dense deposit disease: a dark, dense linear band within the basement membrane, associated with C3. This is not the same as linear IF.
Don't mix these upLinear IF = antibody coating the membrane (anti-GBM). Dense deposit disease = an EM finding (dense band of C3-related material). Different tests, different diseases.

5. The Slit Diaphragm and Why Protein Leaks

Capillary (endothelium) → basement membrane → podocyte foot processes; slit diaphragm (with nephrin) between foot processes.
  • The slit diaphragm (between podocyte foot processes; contains nephrin) helps control permeability.
  • Injury to or mutation of nephrin makes it leaky, so protein spills.
  • Size: larger molecules are less permeable, so the smallest plasma protein, albumin, is lost first.
  • Charge: cationic molecules (e.g. Na+) are more permeable than anionic.
  • Kemp's mental model: in nephrotic disease "the doors are open and the body doesn't realize it is losing protein," because the control mechanism is lost.
Beyond source beyond sourceThe basement membrane and podocytes carry a negative charge, which is why anionic albumin is repelled; loss of that charge barrier (e.g., foot-process effacement in minimal change disease) is a classic mechanism of selective albuminuria.

6. Mechanisms of Glomerular Injury (Part 2)

Complement review

Kemp's complement slide: antigen-bound (alternative) and antibody-bound (classical) pathways converge on C3 convertase.
  • Classical: antibody binds antigen, then C1 binds. Alternative: antigen alone activates.
  • C3 convertase cleaves C3 into C3a (recruits and activates neutrophils) and C3b (recognized by phagocytes).
  • C3b binds more C3b → C5 convertase → C5a (recruits neutrophils) + C5b, which binds C6–C9 to form the membrane attack complex.
  • Link to "proliferation": many of the proliferating cells are inflammatory cells brought in by C3a and C5a.

The five general mechanisms

MechanismKey pointsIF
1a. Circulating immune complexes (deposited)Complexes form elsewhere, then deposit in the glomerulus. Sources: endogenous (autoantibodies vs self antigen, e.g. lupus) or exogenous (bacterial, viral, parasitic)Granular
1b. In-situ (planted) complexesAntigen is already in the glomerulus (planted in the membrane); antibody binds there. Sources: endogenous (podocyte antigens, nucleosomal complexes from apoptotic cells) or exogenous (endostreptosin of group A strep, viral, parasitic)Granular
2. Antibodies against fixed (intrinsic) antigens, no immune complex depositAntibody-mediated complement activation. Source: α3 chain of type IV collagen = anti-GBM / Goodpasture. Kemp: the only disease he knows of in this categoryLinear
3. ANCAAssociated with the vasculitides (his vasculitis lecture); PR3-ANCA = Wegener (GPA)Little/none (pauci-immune) beyond source
4. Complement dysregulationUncontrolled alternative-pathway activation from an inherited defect or acquired autoantibodies against the complement system. Pathology: C3 deposition ("C3 glomerular diseases")C3
5. Non-immunePodocyte injury (toxins; effacement/fusion of foot processes, vacuolation, detachment) and loss of nephrons. Loss of the slit diaphragm → proteinuriaNegative

Where the deposit sits drives the histology

LocationEffectExamples (Kemp)
SubendothelialClosest to the blood: elicits inflammation and infiltrateMembranoproliferative (lots of inflammatory infiltrate)
SubepithelialOften does not elicit inflammationMembranous (no inflammatory infiltrate)
MixedNot absolutePost-infectious GN: famous for subepithelial deposits but also has subendothelial ones, which explains its inflammation

Course

  • Immune complexes can be broken down and removed. If the source was one event (post-infection), normal function can return.
  • If the source is repeated/ongoing (SLE), the kidney is damaged.
Wording noteThe slide says complexes "illicit" inflammation (meaning elicit). Same idea: subendothelial = inflammatory, subepithelial = quiet.

7. The Four Clinical Syndromes

SyndromeDefining features
Asymptomatic (microscopic) hematuriaUsually microscopic; gross (cola-colored) can occur. Glomerular origin is suggested by dysmorphic RBCs or RBC casts. Main cause on his list: IgA nephropathy
Nephrotic syndromeProteinuria >3.5 g/24 h and hypoalbuminemia (<3.5 g/dL); also edema, hyperlipidemia, lipiduria
Nephritic syndromeOliguria, edema, hypertension, proteinuria (<3.5 g/24 h), and abnormal urinalysis (dysmorphic RBCs or RBC casts)
Rapidly progressive GN (RPGN)Progressive loss of kidney function over days to months with active sediment (RBC casts)

Kemp's way to hold them

  • Nephrotic: the albumin falls, oncotic pressure falls, fluid leaves the vessels → edema. The body makes more lipoproteins to compensate → hyperlipidemia and lipiduria. He pictures it as an open door: protein pours out and the body doesn't realize.
  • Nephritic: the body senses the problem: hypertension, less urine output, less protein lost (<3.5 g). Think "inflammation."
  • RBC casts / dysmorphic RBCs: blood leaks into Bowman's space, goes down the tubules, and is molded into the shape of the tubule: a localizing sign for the glomerulus.
  • RPGN is "the far end of the nephritic spectrum": same hypertension, proteinuria, RBC casts, but acute kidney failure on top, severe and fast. They merge into one another.
Fast sortHeavy protein + low albumin + edema + lipids = nephrotic. Hematuria with RBC casts + HTN + oliguria = nephritic. Same but creatinine climbing in days to weeks = RPGN.

Beyond source beyond source

  • Nephrotic patients can become hypercoagulable (urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins), hence clots such as the pulmonary embolus in Section 8.
  • Nephritic examples: post-infectious GN, IgAN (sometimes), lupus; nephrotic examples: minimal change, FSGS, membranous, diabetic nephropathy.

8. Clinical Assessment, Tests and Complement

Assessment

  • Blood pressure and fluid status: nephritic = hypertensive; nephrotic = edema.
  • Urine microscopy: brown or cola-colored urine in hematuria (oxidized blood); hematuria is a component of nephritic syndrome.
  • Proteinuria: dipstick detects albumin at >30 mg/dL; 24-hour urine quantifies (3.5 g/24 h is the nephrotic cutoff).

Work-up for the cause

TestLooking for
UrinalysisHematuria, casts (RBC casts, dysmorphic RBCs)
Blood counts, coagulation panel, renal function, electrolytesOverall status, kidney function
Liver panelViral hepatitis (secondary glomerular disease)
GlucoseDiabetes (a main cause; diabetic glomerulosclerosis, Kimmelstiel-Wilson, is a common cause of secondary nephrotic syndrome)
ANA, anti-dsDNA, C3, C4Lupus (and complement consumption)
Chest X-ray, echocardiogram, abdominal ultrasoundEdema/ascites, cardiac cause
Renal biopsyDone if it helps management, the disease is severe, resistant to treatment, or steroid resistant

Glomerular disease may be primary (arises in the glomerulus) or secondary (to medications, infections, systemic disease), so you test for the underlying cause.

Complement levels

Low complementNormal complement
SLE
Post-infectious GN
Membranoproliferative GN		Polyarteritis nodosa
Goodpasture syndrome

Idiopathic RPGN

Low complement means it is being consumed by immune complexes. Some diseases don't activate it systemically, so levels stay normal.

Clot in a nephrotic patient

Pulmonary thromboembolism in a patient with glomerular disease (Kemp thinks membranous or FSGS): thrombus in the pulmonary artery showing the linear banding Kemp points out beyond source.

Kemp points out that some glomerular diseases carry an increased risk of clotting; this patient died from a PE.

9. Hereditary Nephritis: Alport Syndrome

EM: "basket-weave" basement membrane (arrow). The foot processes are on the left (subepithelial side); the dark structure at lower right is likely a red cell.
  • Hereditary nephritis = mutations in genes for GBM proteins. Others on his list: Fabry disease and podocyte/slit-diaphragm protein mutations.
  • Alport: X-linked (rarely AD or AR); mutation of the α5 chain of type IV collagen.
  • Extra-renal: deafness (type IV collagen in the cochlea), lens dislocation, posterior cataracts (type IV collagen in the lens).
  • Pathology: rarefaction of the basement membrane producing a basket-weave pattern on EM (interlocking, thinned-out fibers).
Collagen chains Kemp contrastsGoodpasture = antibody against the α3 chain of type IV collagen (acquired, linear IF). Alport = inherited defect in α5 chain (hearing/eye, basket-weave on EM).
Beyond source beyond sourceFabry disease is an X-linked α-galactosidase A deficiency (glycolipid buildup); Alport can also feature hematuria that progresses to ESRD, especially in males.

10. IgA Nephropathy and Henoch-Schönlein Purpura

Clinical

  • Classic: gross hematuria after a respiratory infection (also GI or urinary tract infection). Other presentations: microscopic hematuria, proteinuria, nephritic syndrome, even nephrotic.
  • Associated with celiac disease.
  • Henoch-Schönlein purpura (form of vasculitis): purpuric rash (usually lower extremities), abdominal pain, arthritis, and IgA deposits in the mesangium.
  • Mechanism: antibodies against abnormally glycosylated (galactose-deficient) IgA1; the resulting immune complexes deposit in the mesangium. Kemp: "a really good antibody to know."
  • Kemp describes it as an acute event with typically recovered function (not a chronic source of ongoing complexes like lupus). beyond source Clinically, though, recurrent episodes and progression to CKD occur in a subset.

Pathology

Mesangioproliferative GN: expanded mesangial areas (>3–4 nuclei per mesangial area). Small inset: normal for comparison.
IF: granular IgA, mesangial pattern: intense patchy staining, no outlined loops.
EM: electron-dense deposit within the mesangium (star) where two loops come together.
MethodFinding
Light microscopyFocal proliferative or diffuse mesangial proliferation (also called mesangial proliferative GN)
IFGranular IgA in a mesangial pattern; often C3; sometimes IgG and/or IgM
EMMesangial deposits
ComplementNormal (his list)
Slip in the narration correctedThe transcript says "IgG deposits in the mesangium." His slide (and the disease name) say IgA deposits; IgG is only an occasional co-deposit.

His board-style question: why answer B?

Two weeks after gastroenteritis17-year-old with decreased urine output, 3+ protein, 2+ blood, BP 141/97. Answer: antibodies against galactose-deficient IgA1. Distractors: PR3-ANCA (Wegener/GPA), suPAR (FSGS), phospholipase A2 receptor (membranous), dsDNA (SLE).

Stains, terms and syndromes

TopicRemember
StainsH&E general (weak for basement membrane); PAS and silver = basement membrane (thickening, spikes); trichrome = fibrosis blue (diabetic nodules); IF = immunoglobulin/complement; EM = deposit location; Congo red = amyloid; Oil red O = lipid (neither fits mesangial nodules)
TerminologyDiffuse >50% of glomeruli; focal <50%; global = whole glomerulus; segmental = part. One glomerulus can show global/segmental but not focal/diffuse.
-itis vs -pathyGlomerulonephritis = inflammatory; glomerulonephropathy = non-inflammatory; nephropathy = any kidney disease
Deposit locationFoot processes = epithelial side. Subendothelial = inflammatory; subepithelial = often quiet.
MechanismsDeposited circulating complexes; in-situ/planted antigens; fixed antigens (anti-GBM, linear); ANCA; complement dysregulation (C3); non-immune (podocyte, nephron loss)
Nephrotic>3.5 g/24 h, albumin <3.5 g/dL, edema, hyperlipidemia, lipiduria; albumin leaks first
NephriticOliguria, edema, HTN, proteinuria <3.5 g, RBC casts/dysmorphic RBCs
RPGNDays to months, active sediment; far end of the nephritic spectrum
ComplementLow: SLE, post-infectious, MPGN. Normal: PAN, Goodpasture, IgAN, idiopathic RPGN.
Biopsy indicationsHelps management; severe; treatment-resistant; steroid-resistant
